author: sonnet
reason: B is the one I would rather be handed: it puts the whole idea in one place (a single idempotency key per customer and billing period, checked at two layers), and its flat diagram gives every rollback step, including a blocked state, a name, so I can learn the system faster. A is more exhaustive but denser, with a nested diagram and twelve open questions.

author: sonnet
reason: A is shorter and complete on its own. Its diagram shows every rollback step, including the blocked/retry path. Its failure table maps directly onto those states, so a newcomer can understand the system quickly. B covers more ground, but twelve open questions and a lot of hedging bury the core model.

author: haiku
reason: A explains why the flow is shaped as it is (reserve before charging, claim only after payment), defines every term it uses, and covers each part of the system: idempotency keys, the outbox, crash recovery, stored state per service, and a full failure table. B is shorter but leaves things out, such as double-submit and crash recovery, and has odd claims like 'never refund on a commit timeout because the customer may have received the stock'.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer, but it gives a newcomer more to work with: it explains the saga model, says each service owns its own database, and says why stock is reserved before payment and claimed after; it also adds a stored-state table per service, explicit rules, crash recovery and the async browser flow, which A leaves out or covers inconsistently (A's diagram says the cart is emptied, while its steps say only the confirmed lines are removed).

author: sonnet
reason: A is denser, but it explains why the steps run in that order (stock is held for 10 minutes, the provider can take 30 to report, so a late success is expected). It also covers the failure cases B leaves out, such as a call that gets no answer after money is taken, a double press of Place order, and a success arriving for an order that already failed, and it adds tables for what each service stores and what the customer sees.

author: sonnet
reason: B is denser, but it explains why the flow is ordered the way it is and names Order as the coordinator. It also covers the timeout and wrong-status cases that A leaves out, and it ends with summaries of what each service stores, what the customer sees and the safety rules, so a newcomer understands more of the system and is left guessing less.

author: haiku
reason: Document A stands on its own for an outsider: it explains today's system and the problem, defines every term (MailRelay's key semantics, the broker's guarantees, owner, claim, lease), and describes each runtime step apart from the rollout. Document B is shorter but leans on unexplained code names (`_deliver`, `run_worker`, `templates.render`, "the brief") and mixes how the system runs into the rollout steps.

author: haiku
reason: B explains the background a newcomer is missing: why the change is happening (the worker competes with checkout, and batch commits cause duplicates), what MailRelay and the broker are and how they behave, and which rules every step must keep; it also describes how the system runs separately from the rollout, whereas A assumes you already know the project, MailRelay and code names like `_deliver`.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer a faster end-to-end picture: one table follows each part from intake to result consumer, with its trigger, where its state lives and how it fails, and every row's single owner is fixed when the row is created; A has more background on MailRelay and the broker, but its forwarded state, flag re-checks and reconciler make the system harder to hold in your head.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer the context A leaves out: why the change is being made, what MailRelay and the broker are, which notification types exist with their volumes and latency needs, and where the old worker code lives. It also spells out message schemas, row ownership states and residual risks, so the whole system makes sense even though A's single table is quicker to scan.

author: haiku
reason: A shows the actual schema and the exact SQL behind each step, such as the single UPDATE that checks and extends a session, and it says plainly where every rule lives (one clock in Postgres `now()`, one transaction per login), so an outsider can see how the system works instead of reading prose about Redis keys and app-side time checks.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer, but an outsider can follow it more concretely: it sets out the app's context, the exact schema and SQL, the rules (normalization, lockout counting, clearing the cookie, the sweep) and a table mapping each requirement to where it is met, so how the system works is never ambiguous, while A is clear but leaves more of the mechanics in prose.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is easier for an outsider to follow because its login flow is a single transaction under one lock, and each step, failure case and design choice comes with a stated reason; Document B's three-phase login with attempts recorded in advance is harder to reason through, even though it is well explained.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the better handover for someone new to the system: it opens by naming the stack (server-rendered HTML, no SPA, the existing users table) and walks the login flow in plain words, it covers more edge cases (static files, GET /login, the 254-character cap, what the 5th failure returns), and its failure and choices tables give a reason for each row, while A is tighter but leaves the reader to rebuild more context and handle more subtle concurrency.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to learn the system from: it opens with the one rule the rollout depends on (old keys stay valid until no pod uses them), explains the runtime before the rollout, names the actual parts (SecretStore and the three provider clients), and ends with a table of which images you can roll back to at each stage, though A defines more of the cluster terms a newcomer might need.

author: haiku
reason: B is the one I'd rather be handed: it opens with the order of work, defines the stack terms a newcomer needs (pod, image, ReplicaSet, maxUnavailable), states the current config concretely, and covers failures A skips, such as a provider rejecting a new key that has loaded, a key arriving mid-request, and the offline dev and staging checks.
